# Google

This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the <term>copyright<note>The legal right that grants the creator of a work exclusive control over its use and distribution for a set period of time.</note></term> to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain<note>A status belonging to creative works upon which no intellectual property rights apply, making them free for anyone to use or distribute.</note></term>. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that’s often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia<note>original: "marginalia"; these are handwritten notes, sketches, or comments made by previous readers in the blank spaces surrounding the text of a book.</note></term> present in the original volume will appear in this file — a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

### **Usage guidelines**

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on <term>automated querying<note>The use of software or "bots" to automatically search or download large amounts of data without human intervention.</note></term>.

We also ask that you:

+ **Make non-commercial use of the files** We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.
+ **Refrain from automated querying** Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.
+ **Maintain attribution** The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.
+ **Keep it legal** Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

### **About Google Book Search**

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. **A**CCORDING to classical legend, the Goddess Athena <note>The Greek goddess of wisdom, craft, and war, often representing the intellectual or spiritual aspect of humanity.</note> had once for votary <note>A person, such as a monk or nun, who has made vows of dedication to religious service.</note> a fair virgin named Medusa, who, becoming vain of her beauty and weary of the pure service of the maiden Goddess, introduced folly and defilement into the very sanctuary of the Temple in which she was wont to worship. Thereupon a terrible fate overtook her ; the beautiful face, which had been the cause of her fall, assumed an aspect so terrible as to blight and petrify all who looked upon it ; her tresses, once the chief object of her pride, were changed into vipers ; and the hands which had ministered to heaven became as the talons of a bird of prey. Thus transformed into a Gorgon, <note>In Greek mythology, a monstrous female creature; Medusa is the most famous of the three Gorgon sisters.</note> she brought forth monsters, and for a time devastated the earth. At length the hero Perseus, “Son of God,” <note>In the myth, Perseus is the son of Zeus (the king of the gods) and the mortal Danaë. The authors use the phrase "Son of God" here to highlight a mystical or allegorical parallel between Greek myth and Christian theology.</note> commissioned by Athena and Hermes, <note>The messenger of the gods, associated with transitions and boundaries.</note> and armed by them with wings and sword and shield, slew the terrible

The teachings that originally bore the mark of the divine and reflected Heavenly Wisdom herself have, through the corruption of the Church, been turned into dogmas so harmful and lethal that they ruin the intellect of anyone who follows them. In this myth, Perseus represents true Humanity—born of the earth but fathered by heaven—who is gifted by Wisdom and Understanding with the wings of Courage, the shield of Intuition, and the sword of <term>Science</term> <note>In this context, "Science" refers to *Scientia*—sacred, certain knowledge of spiritual laws rather than modern physical science.</note>. He has set out to strike down the corrupt Church and free the world from its poisonous influence.

But killing the <term>Gorgon</term> <note>The Medusa, who symbolizes the "dead letter" of religious dogma that turns the living spirit into stone.</note> is not enough. A task even greater and more glorious remains to be done. <term>Andromeda</term>, who represents the <term>Soul</term>—the higher part of Man—is on the verge of being swallowed whole by the destructive dragon of <term>Negation</term> <note>The spirit of denial or materialism that rejects the existence of the soul.</note>, which acts as the agent of our lower nature and destroys all human hope. Her name—which corresponds to the terms used to describe the first Woman in the Hebrew tradition—shows that she is the partner and ruler of man. Her ancestry shows that the Soul originates from the astral Fire or **Aether** <note>The "fifth element" or quintessence; a subtle, celestial substance once believed to fill the space beyond the earth's atmosphere.</note>, represented here by the land of Ethiopia. The bronze chains binding her to the rock symbolize the current state of the divine element in humanity, which is enslaved by its material body. Her rescue, marriage, and elevation by the hero Perseus represent the ultimate triumph of the "Son of God." This "Son" is nothing other than Human Reason, strengthened and supported by Wisdom and...

Thought. The old methods of fear, persecution, and slavery—once used by the corrupt Church to force people into its beliefs—are useless against the monster that threatens to destroy the human Soul. The Deliverer of the Soul must be as free as the air, carried on the wings of a Thought that knows no fear or restriction. He must be armed with the blade of a knowledge that penetrates everything—a sharp edge that no religious dogma, no matter how stubborn, can blunt. This deliverer must be wise and free in every sense, focused not just on destroying evil, but on saving what is good. His sword must be just as ready to cut the chains from the limbs of <term>Andromeda</term> <note>Representing the human Soul or the higher, spiritual self.</note> as it is to deal the death blow to the <term>Gorgon</term> <note>Representing the "dead letter" of religious dogma that paralyzes the mind.</note>.

It is not enough for him to bring the head of the dead Medusa to <term>Olympus</term> <note>The home of the gods; here representing the state of spiritual perfection or the divine realm.</note>; he must also bring a living Bride. His mission is to satisfy both the Mind and the Heart. The **Intellect**—symbolized as "Man"—is the one who wields the sword of liberation. However, it is the **Intuition**—symbolized as "Woman"—who weaves and builds. Without her labor, the hero's bravery would be useless, and his actions would have no purpose or reward. The hero brings his prizes home to the tent and hangs his shield and spear by the fire. We must give all honor to this warrior, whether he acts as an **iconoclast** <note>One who destroys established religious images or cherished but outdated beliefs.</note>, a scientist, or a purifier of the world. Yet, his work is only the beginning. He is merely preparing the way and smoothing the path for *Her* who carries neither a torch nor a weapon of war. By her, the intellect is crowned; by her, humanity is made whole; in her the Son of

<term>Zeus</term> <note>The king of the Greek gods, used here to symbolize the supreme Divine Source.</note> finds his eternal and supreme reward; for she is the shrine at once of divinest Wisdom and of perfect Love.

It is thus evident that classical story, identical in substance with the allegorical prophecies of Hebrew and Christian scripture, exhibits the work of the Saviour or Liberator, as having a twofold character. Like Zeus the Father of Spirits, whose son he is, the **Reason** is at once Purifier and Redeemer. The task of Destruction accomplished, that of Reconstruction must begin. Already the first is well-nigh complete, but as yet no one seems to have dreamed of the last as possible. The present age has witnessed the decline and fall of a system which, after having successfully maintained itself for some eighteen centuries against innumerable perils of assault from without and of faction from within, has at length succumbed to the combined arms of scientific and moral criticism. But this very overthrow, this very demolition, creates a new void, to the existence of which the present condition of the world and the apprehensions and cravings everywhere expressed, bear ample testimony. On all sides, are men asking themselves, “Who will show us any good?” To whom or to what, if the old system be fallen, shall we turn for counsel and salvation from Doom? Under what roof shall we shelter ourselves if the whole Temple be demolished, and “not one stone be left upon another that shall not be <note>This is a biblical allusion to Matthew 24:2, referring here to the total collapse of traditional religious structures under the weight of modern scrutiny.</note>

<summary>This page argues that the historical destruction of dogmatic religious systems by modern science and morality has left a spiritual void. It suggests that human Reason must now move beyond its role as a "Purifier" (destroyer of falsehoods) to become a "Redeemer" (builder of a new spiritual home).</summary>

The certainty of their attainment is involved in the nature itself of existence, and ratified in every expression given to the <term>mysteries of that nature</term> <note>A reference to the "Ancient Mysteries"—the hidden spiritual truths and initiation rites found in various historical traditions.</note> from the beginning of the world.

-># PREFACE.<-

of destruction has been widely and amply rendered. The old Temple has been thrown down and despoiled, and the “children of Israel” have been carried away captive to “Babylon,”—the mystic name of the stronghold of <term>Materialism</term> <note>In this context, materialism refers to the philosophical view that only physical matter exists, denying the reality of the soul or spirit.</note>. As it is written; “The vessels of the House of the Lord,”—that is, the doctrines of the Church,—“great and small, and the treasures of the Temple and of the King and of the princes, were carried away to Babylon. And the enemies set fire to the House of God, and broke down the wall of Jerusalem,”—that is, the <term>Soul</term> <note>The authors interpret the physical city of Jerusalem as a symbol for the human soul or the internal spiritual state.</note>,—“and burnt all her towers, and whatsoever was precious they destroyed.”

Time it is now for the fulfilment of the second and last act of the prophetical drama;—

> “Thus saith Cyrus,”—that is, <term>The Lord <note>original: Κύριος (Kyrios). The authors are making a wordplay between the name of the Persian King Cyrus and the Greek word for 'Lord.'</note></term>, the Christ;—“All the kingdoms of the earth hath the God of heaven given me, and He hath charged me to build Him again a House in Jerusalem.” “Who is there of you, who will go up and build again the Temple of the Lord God of Israel?”

## LECTURE THE FIRST.
### *INTRODUCTORY.*

32. The doctrine of creation by development or evolution is a true doctrine; but the development is not of the original <term>substance<note>In this philosophical context, "Substance" refers to the underlying, eternal divine essence of the universe, rather than just physical matter.</note></term>. Being infinite and eternal, that is perfect always. Development is of the manifestation of the qualities of that substance *in the individual*.

Development is intelligible only by the recognition of the inherent consciousness of the substance of existence. Of the qualities of that substance as manifested in the individual, Form is the expression. And it is because development is directed by conscious, experienced, and continually experiencing intelligence, which is ever seeking to eliminate the rudimentary and imperfect, that progression occurs in respect of Form. The highest product, man, is the result of the Spirit working intelligently within. But man attains his highest, and becomes perfect only through his own voluntary co-operation with the Spirit.

There is no mode of Matter in which the potentiality of personality, and therein of man, does not subsist. For every molecule is a mode of the universal consciousness. Without consciousness is no being. For consciousness *is* being.

37. The doctrine of the <term>Progression and Migration of Souls<note>Also known as metempsychosis or reincarnation, this is the belief that the soul moves through a series of different bodies—animal, human, and divine—over many lifetimes to achieve spiritual perfection.</note></term>, and of the power of man, while still in the body, to recover the recollections of his soul, constituted the foundation of all those ancient religions out of which Christianity had its birth; and was therefore universally communicated to all initiates of the <term>sacred mysteries<note>The "Mysteries" were secret religious schools in the ancient world—such as those at Eleusis or in Egypt—where students were taught spiritual truths through symbolic rituals and intensive study.</note></term>. *f.* If it be, indeed, that man is not to "go down quick into the pit" that he has dug for himself, the emergency is one with which religion alone can grapple. But, so far from the religion already in the world being competent for the task, it has, by reason of its own degeneracy, ministered to the evil. Wherefore only by a religion which is not that now in vogue, can man be saved. Time can, of course, alone determine if, or by what means, the needed **redemption** <note>The restoration of humanity to its spiritual nature.</note> will be wrought. Enough has been said to show that, from the religious point of view, there is ample reason in favour of according a serious hearing even to doctrines and claims so strange and unfamiliar to most persons as those herein advanced.

# INTRODUCTORY LECTURE.

56. Finally, to close this Introductory Lecture, and to reassure those who, desirous to know more, are yet apprehensive of finding themselves in the issue, like the patriarch of old, robbed of their gods, <note>A reference to the biblical story of Micah (Judges 18:24), who cried out when his sacred idols were taken. The authors use this to address the fear that critical study might destroy a person's faith.</note> we add this final reflection:— The end in view is not denial, but interpretation; not destruction, but reconstruction, and this with the very materials hitherto in use. No names, personages, or doctrines now regarded as divine will be rejected or defamed. And even though the indubitable fact be recognised, that the “one name given under heaven whereby men can be saved” <note>Quoting Acts 4:12, a traditional Christian reference to Jesus.</note> has been shared by many, that name will still be the name of salvation, and the symbol of its triumph will still be the cross of Jesus, even though borne before him by, or in the name of, an <term>Osiris</term> <note>The Egyptian god of the afterlife and rebirth.</note>, a <term>Mithras</term> <note>A Persian deity associated with the sun and a prominent mystery religion in the Roman Empire.</note>, a <term>Crishna</term> <note>Now commonly spelled Krishna; a major Hindu deity and avatar of Vishnu.</note>, a <term>Dionysus</term> <note>The Greek god of wine and ecstasy, often associated in mystical traditions with rebirth.</note>, or a <term>Buddha</term> <note>The "Enlightened One," Siddhartha Gautama, founder of Buddhism.</note>, or any others who, overcoming by love the limitations of **Matter**, have been faithful to the death mystically called the death of the cross, and, attaining thereby the crown of eternal life for themselves, have shown to men the way of salvation.

Instead, then, of indulging apprehension on the score indicated, let heed rather be given to the true moral of the story of all the <term>Christs</term>, how many soever they be, by whom is enacted in its fulness, while yet in the body, the divine drama of the soul. For, with Christ, all may, in their degree, be redeemers alike of themselves and of others; and with him, to redeem, they must themselves first love and suffer and die. For, as said the German mystic, <term>Scheffler</term> <note>Johannes Scheffler (1624–1677), also known as Angelus Silesius, a priest and poet known for his mystical verses.</note>, two centuries ago,—

> “Though Christ a thousand times in <term>Bethlehem</term> be born,
> But not within thyself, thy soul will be forlorn:
> The cross of <term>Golgotha</term> <note>The site of the crucifixion; here used to symbolize external or historical sacrifice.</note> thou lookest to in vain,
> Unless within thyself it be set up again.”

# LECTURE THE SECOND.

## *THE SOUL; AND THE SUBSTANCE OF EXISTENCE.*

### PART I.

1. OUR theme is that which is at once the supreme subject and object of culture, <note>In this context, "culture" refers to the cultivation of the mind and spirit rather than just social customs.</note> and the necessary basis of all real religion and science. For it is the substance of existence, the Soul, universal and individual, of humanity. Only when we know the nature of this, can we know what we ourselves are, and what we have it in us to become. For our potentialities necessarily depend upon the substance whereof we are made.

2. This is not **Matter**. Wherefore a science which, in being restricted to the cognition of phenomena, <note>Phenomena refers to things as they appear to our senses, rather than their underlying reality.</note> is a materialistic science, cannot help us to an understanding of ourselves. But, on the contrary, to such understanding such science is, in its issues, the greatest enemy. **Matter** is not God; and in order to understand ourselves, it is necessary to understand God. God is the <term>Substance</term> <note>From the Latin *substantia*, meaning "that which stands under." In philosophy, substance is the fundamental reality that supports all outward qualities.</note> of existence. Be that substance what it may, it still is God; and of God no other definition is possible or desirable, but all conditions are satisfied by it. To know God, then, is to know this substance; and to know this, is to know ourselves, and only by knowing this can we know ourselves.

3. Such, and no other or less, was the meaning of the famous mystic utterance inscribed on the temple porch at Delphi,—*Know thyself*, <note>original: "Gnothi Seauton." A famous Ancient Greek aphorism famously associated with the Oracle at Delphi.</note>—a sentence which, notwithstanding

->## THE PERFECT WAY.<-

In terms of all the qualities and properties that make up **Being**, we must contrast it with the total absence of those qualities, which we call **Not-being**. Divine creation must exist between these two polar opposites. There is no other way for God to be fully revealed than through this extreme contrast. The darkness of God's shadow <note>In this context, the "shadow" refers to the physical, material world which seems dark compared to the pure light of the spirit.</note> must be just as intense as the brightness of God's light. We can only truly understand and value one by having a full knowledge of the other. Only a person who has a deep, firsthand knowledge of evil can truly appreciate what is good. 

It is a profound truth that "the greater the sinner, the greater the saint." That perfect summary of the **Soul's** history—the parable of the **Prodigal Son**—is based on this same idea. <note>The parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32) is used here as an allegory for the soul's journey: leaving the divine home to experience the world, and returning with greater wisdom.</note> Only those who have gone out from God and returned can truly know God. **Matter** is both the result and the cause of this "going out" from God. It is an essential servant to Creation; without Matter and the boundaries it sets, Creation could not exist.

10. However, the act of physical Creation alone does not represent the full extent of the Divine purpose. A creation that was limited only to the physical realities of **Matter** would be a curse to itself and no credit to God. If the **Deity** <note>A term for God or the Divine essence.</note> only created physical things, it would prove itself to be only what the **Materialist** <note>One who believes that nothing exists except matter and its movements/modifications.</note> imagines it to be: namely, mere physical **Force**. 

But "God is **Love**." And **Love** is not something that simply creates a thing, gives it a brief caress, and then rejects or throws it away. Instead, Love is that which supports, saves, perfects, and makes things eternal. **Matter** is an indispensable tool for these goals. It contributes to a "second creation" which serves as the supplement and completion of the first. This second creation is called ***Redemption***, and it is through this process that the Creator is recognized and glorified, and man finds his own perfection and eternal life. # THE PERFECT WAY.

15. The plane on which the celestial beings and earthly creatures touch each other is the <term>astral plane</term><note>A subtle level of reality that acts as a bridge between the physical world and the purely spiritual realm.</note>. The soul, being eternal in its essence, passes from one physical form to another until, in its most advanced stage, it <term>polarises</term><note>Aligns its energy or focus, much like a magnet, to become a receptive vessel for the divine spirit.</note> sufficiently to receive the spirit. The soul exists in all organized things. Nothing that has an organic nature exists without a soul. It is the very essence of the **individual**, and it eventually perishes if it is not <term>uninformed of the spirit</term><note>In this context, "uninformed" means the soul has not been shaped, filled, or given life-sustaining form by the higher divine spirit.</note>.

16. This becomes easily understood if we think of God as a vast spiritual body made up of many individual elements, all sharing a single will and therefore being one. This state of oneness with the Divine Will and Being is what, in <term>Hindu mysticism</term><note>A reference to the spiritual traditions of India, which were of great interest to 19th-century occultists and philosophers.</note>, is called the celestial <term>Nirvâna</term><note>original: "Nirvâna". A Sanskrit term usually meaning "blowing out" or "extinction." Here, the author uses it to mean a state of supreme liberation and union with God.</note>. But even though the individual becomes pure Spirit, or God, they still retain their individuality. So, rather than everything simply being swallowed up into the One, the One expresses itself through the Many. In this way, God becomes millions. “God is multitudes, and nations, and kingdoms, and tongues; and the voice of God is as the sound of many waters.”<note>This is a paraphrase of descriptions of the Divine found in the biblical Book of Revelation.</note>

17. So is it with the soul of him who nourishes the Spirit. It grows gradually pure, and becomes Spirit. By this spirit the body is enlightened as a lamp by the flame within it. Now, the flame is not the oil, for the oil may be there without the light; yet the flame cannot be there without the oil. The body, then, is the lamp-case, into which the oil is poured; and this, the oil, is the soul, a fine and combustible fluid; and the flame is the <term>Divine Spirit</term><note>The "Spirit" here refers to the actual presence of the Divine, while the "soul" is the medium through which that Spirit acts in the physical world.</note>, which is not born of the oil, but is communicated by God from within. We may quench this Spirit utterly, and thenceforward we shall have no immortality; but when the lamp-case breaks, the oil will be spilt on the earth, and a few fumes will for a time arise from it, and then it will expend itself, leaving at last no trace. Thus, as in the parable of the Talents, where God has given five talents, man pays back ten; or he pays back nothing and perishes.

And the terrestrial, or kingdom of this world, which consists of astral body—the seat of the <term>animal soul</term> <note>original: *anima bruta*; refers to the lower, instinctive soul shared with the animal kingdom.</note>—and of phenomenal body, is without. Of these two dualisms, each is to the other the *Beyond*. And between them, saving only where one and the same Divine Will,—the will which has its seat in, and which is, the Spirit,—pervades the whole being, is antagonism. They are respectively the spiritual man and the natural man. But in the suffusion of the entire personality thus constituted, by one and the same Divine Will, consists what mystically is termed the <term>At-one-ment</term>, or reconciliation between man and God, but which is commonly called the <term>Atonement</term>. <note>The authors use the hyphenated "At-one-ment" to emphasize that the word originally means the state of being "at one" or in harmony, rather than just a payment for sins.</note>

4. As the whole is, thus, fourfold, so, with the exception of the spirit, are the parts. The external, material body, whether of planet or of man, is fourfold in that it is gaseous, mineral, vegetable, animal. The astral body, or <term>perisoul</term> <note>A term for the "envelope" or surrounding layer of the soul.</note>, is fourfold, being magnetic, purgatorial, limbic, cherubic—terms presently to be explained. The soul is fourfold, namely, elemental, instinctive, vital, rational.

6. These circuli correspond to **Air**, **Water**, **Earth**, and **Fire**, beginning at the outer and uppermost and going inwards and downwards. God alone is Life, or the principle of eternal generation. And, as Life, God comprises all things necessary to life, to its production, that is, to its perfection, and to its perpetuation. God, while giving to all the opportunity and choice, compels no one to remain in Being. God accepts only willing service; and there is no such thing as compulsory salvation. God,—that is Good,—must be loved and followed for the sake of God and Good, not through fear of possible penalties, or hope of possible rewards.

The man who sullies his humanity by cruelty or impurity, is already below the grade of humanity; and the form which his soul assumes is the mere natural consequence of that degradation. Form is the expression of qualities. These are dependent upon the condition of substance, so that the soul takes necessarily its form according to its condition. And this is dependent upon the will or affections of the individual. Wherefore it is an error to hold “Nature” responsible for fierce and horrible creatures. All that “Nature” does, is to enable creatures to take form according to the image in which they have made themselves by the tendencies they have voluntarily encouraged. She allows that which is interior to the individual to manifest itself exteriorly. Were this not so, no character of any creature could be known by its appearance. "spirits" are mere vehicles, and are no more possessed of independent volition or motive than is the electric current by which telegraphic messages are conveyed, and which, like them, is a medium of thought; or than the air, which, according to circumstances, transmits the germs of health or of disease. The most powerful of them are the salamanders, or fire-spirits. The ability of the elementals to produce physical phenomena, and their lack of any moral sense, render them dangerous. In this they differ from the celestial spirits, for to these no physical demonstration is possible, as they do not come into contact with Matter.

37. But first, in order the better to comprehend the procession of Spirit, it should be explained that Life may be represented by a triangle, at the apex of which is God. Of this triangle the two sides are formed by two streams, the one flowing outwards, the other upwards. The base may be taken to represent the material plane. Thus, from God proceed the **Gods**, the **<term>Elohim</term>** <note>Hebrew: *Elohim*; a plural name for God, interpreted here as the diverse divine powers or active agents through which the One God creates the universe.</note>, or divine powers, who are the active agents of creation. From the Gods proceed all the hierarchy of heaven, with the various orders from the highest to the lowest. And the lowest are the orders of the **<term>genii</term>** <note>Latin: plural of *genius*; guardian spirits or protective guides assigned to a person, place, or thing.</note>, or guardian angels. These rest on the astral plane, but do not enter it. The other side of the triangle is a continuation of the base. And herein is the significance alike of the pyramid and of the obelisk. The pyramid represents the triangle of Life, fourfold, and resting on the earth. The obelisk, the summit only of which is pyramidal, represents a continuation of the base, and is covered with sculptured forms of animal life. For, of this

42. The **<term>Genius</term>** <note>Latin: *genius*; a protective spirit or "inner spark" believed in Roman religion to accompany a person through life.</note> of a man is this satellite. 43. It is in virtue of man's being a planet that he has a moon. If he were not fourfold, as is the planet, he could not have one. Rudimentary men are not fourfold. They have not the Spirit.

44. Every human spirit-soul has attached to him a genius, variously called, by Socrates, a **<term>dæmon</term>** <note>Greek: *daimōn*; a guiding spirit. 45. 46. The genius knows well only the things relating to the person to whom he ministers. About other things he has opinions only. The relation of the ministering spirit to his client, is very well represented by that of the Catholic **confessor** to his penitent. He is bound to keep towards every penitent profound secrecy as regards the affairs of other souls. If this were not the case, there would be no order, and no secret would be safe. The genius of each one knows about another person only so much as that other's genius chooses to reveal.

55. For the **Nous** has become one with the soul, and the cord of union is dis-solved. And yet again, the three become twain at the dissolution of the body; and again, the twain become one, that is, the Christ-spirit-soul. The Divine Spirit and the genius, therefore, are not to be regarded as diverse, nor yet as identical. The genius is flame, and is celestial; that is, he is Spirit, and one in nature with the Divine; for his light is the Divine Light. ## LECTURE THE FOURTH.

### ***THE <term>ATONEMENT</term>*** <note>Historically understood as "at-one-ment," this term refers to the reconciliation or restoration of harmony between humanity and the Divine.</note>

#### PART I.

1. WE have chosen to speak thus early in our series of the doctrine of the **Atonement**, because it is that around which all religious teaching, ancient and modern, pure and corrupt, is alike grouped, and in which it all centres. Constituting thus the **pivot and point of radiation** of **Religion** itself, this doctrine, expounded in its pure and ancient sense, is at once the glory of the **saint** and the hope of the **fallen**; expounded in its modern and corrupt sense, it is to the latter a **licence** <note>Here, "licence" refers to the dangerous idea that one has permission to act immorally because they believe a divine sacrifice has already "paid" for their sins.</note>, and to the former a shame and perplexity.

2. As will by-and-by be fully shown, **sacred <term>Mysteries</term>** <note>The inner, spiritual meanings of religious rituals and doctrines, which in ancient times were often kept secret from the uninitiated.</note> are, like all things **<term>cosmic</term>** <note>Relating to the "Cosmos," or the universe understood as an orderly, harmonious system governed by law.</note>, ***fourfold***, in that they contain, like the **whorls of a flower** <note>The circular arrangement of petals or leaves around a central point, used here as a metaphor for layers of meaning.</note>, or the elements of an organic cell, four mutually related and yet distinct **Modes and Ideas**. And these four are—from without inwards—the **Physical**, the **Intellectual**, the **Personal**, and the **Spiritual**. We propose in this lecture to explain the doctrine of the **Atonement** from each of these points of view, in order to do which with clearness and without fear of misapprehension, we shall first expose the common errors in regard to it.

The key-note of **Religion** is sounded in the words, "*My kingdom is not of this world.*" <note>original Latin: "Regnum meum non est de hoc mundo" (John 18:36). The **Soul** is the true and only person concerned; and any relation which **Religion** may have to the body or physical man, is indirect, and by **<term>correspondence</term>** <note>A philosophical concept where physical things are seen as mirrors or symbols of higher spiritual realities.</note> only. It is for the **Soul** that the **Divine Word** <note>Often referring to the "Logos" or the spiritual wisdom contained within sacred texts.</note> is written; and it is her nature, her history, her functions, her conflicts, her redemption, which are ever the theme of sacred narrative, prophecy, and doctrine.

1. **THE** argument to the exposition of which this discourse will be devoted, is based on the doctrine of <term>Correspondence</term> <note>A central concept in Hermetic and Swedenborgian philosophy, suggesting that every physical object or event in the "outer" world is a reflection of a spiritual reality in the "inner" world.</note> subsisting between things manifest to the inner sense and things manifest to the outer sense : "the invisible things of God being," as <term>Paul</term> <note>The Apostle Paul; the specific reference is to the Book of Romans 1:20.</note> says, "understood by the things that are made." <note>original Latin: "Invisibilia enim ipsius, a creatura mundi, per ea quae facta sunt, intellecta, conspiciuntur."</note>

Now the reasonableness and necessity of this doctrine of Correspondence between the outer and the inner, between the real and the material, become apparent when we consider the essential unity of both,—unity, that is, of <term>Substance</term>, <note>In this philosophical context, "Substance" refers to the fundamental "stuff" of the universe—the underlying reality that remains constant beneath all changing appearances.</note> implying unity of origin and of mode.

2. As has already been advanced, the Real is substance in its condition of spirit or Mind ; and the <term>Phenomenal</term> <note>From the Greek word for "appearance." 12. The <term>Cell</term><note>The basic structural and functional unit of all living organisms.</note>, thus constituted, is the basis of every living <term>economy</term><note>In this context, the organized system or functioning of a living body.</note>. 13. A cell, in its completest expression, consists, from without inwards, of cell-membrane, <term>protoplasmic</term><note>Relating to protoplasm, the colorless, jelly-like living part of a cell, including the cytoplasm and nucleus.</note> contents, nucleus, and nucleolus. On the subject of this membrane innumerable discussions have arisen among <term>histologists</term><note>Scientists who study the microscopic structure of tissues.</note>, some maintaining it to be an independent isolable envelope, possessing special chemical qualities, and separable from the cell either by mechanical expression <note>The act of squeezing or pressing something out.</note>, or, as in the fat-cell, by dissolving out the contents by the aid of chemical agents—alcohol or ether; others affirming it to consist only of a hardening or coagulation by concentration, more or less pronounced, of the external surface of the protoplasmic substance, constituting thus a periphery identical in nature with the protoplasm itself. This latter view is now generally accepted. Formerly, too, it was deemed impossible for a cell to exist without a capsular membrane; now it is known that this envelope is often missing, and that its <term>physiological</term><note>Relating to the way in which a living organism or bodily part functions.</note> value is relative merely.

14. The composition of the <term>*protoplasm*</term><note>The colorless, jelly-like living material that fills a cell.</note>, or fluidic content of the cell, undergoes variations according to the age of the cell. At first it is formed only of <term>albuminoid</term><note>Protein-based substances resembling egg white.</note> substance; but later, the processes of <term>assimilation</term><note>The process of absorbing nutrients and turning them into living tissue.</note> and of <term>disassimilation</term><note>The breaking down of tissues to produce energy and waste; modernly called catabolism.</note> which occur in and by it, give rise,—either by <term>intussusception</term><note>A biological term for growth achieved by depositing new particles between existing ones.</note>, or by internal generation,—to the production in its mass of diverse granulations, pigmentary, fatty, and other. The proportion borne by the protoplasmic contents of a cell to its other constituent parts varies with the kind of cell, and with its age and circumstances. Under certain conditions, this plasmic medium may,—as in old <term>epithelial</term><note>Cells that form the surface of the skin and the linings of internal organs.</note> cells on the extreme surface of the skin,—become by degrees wholly solidified, incapable of exercising its normal functions, and transformed into a fixed horny mass known to anatomists as "<term>keratine</term><note>Now spelled keratin; the tough protein found in hair, nails, and the outer skin.</note>." This mass is formed by the intimate merging of the nucleus, cell-membrane, and transformed fluidic body, all of which have become indistinguishable and inseparable one from another, the hardening mass of the degraded protoplasm having gradually absorbed alike the nucleus and the periphery. Such cells are no longer capable of self-perpetuation; they gradually detach themselves, and are shed from the <term>economy</term><note>The organized system or functioning of the living body.</note> of which they were once living elements.

This substance differs in quality from that of the protoplasmic fluid surrounding it, with which it is prevented from fusing by a capsule so tenuous and <term>diaphanous</term><note>Extremely thin, delicate, and translucent.</note> that its presence, even under the strongest lens power, is demonstrated chiefly by the current observable in its contents.

## PART II.

20. We now pass to the second part of our study, namely, the history of the behaviour, or evolution, of the Cell. The **nucleus** was long ago demonstrated,—at least in the greater number of cases,—to exist prior to the formation of the cell itself as a complete entity, of which it has therefore been considered by many observers as the necessary point of departure. But it is only very recently that the entire history of the cell, from its earliest to its latest stages, has been consecutively traced and chronicled.

21. The *Journal of the Royal Microscopical Society* for June, 1879, contains a paper which had been previously read before the Society by two well-known students of <term>histology</term><note>The study of the microscopic structure of tissues in plants and animals.</note>, on the development and retrogression of the typical cell.
The authors of this careful study have assured themselves that all fixed or stationary cells have once been “wandering” cells, that is, nomadic embryonic entities moving over the free surfaces of membranes, in search of some medium or tissue for which they have a physiological affinity, and which, when met with, they will penetrate, by passing from the upper free surface of the membrane into the <term>endothelium-covered tract</term><note>An area lined with a thin layer of cells (endothelium) that usually forms the interface between blood or lymph and the rest of the vessel wall.</note> wherein alone fixed cells are found. Here they will root themselves, and take on the character of “fixed” cells, becoming through contiguity, or some other cause, similar to the other fixed cells of the tissue into which they have been drawn. Young wandering cells, just entering on the migratory stage, consist of a nucleus surrounded by a mere film of <term>protoplasm</term><note>The living, jelly-like substance that makes up the bulk of a cell.</note> or cell-substance, but having no peripheral envelope. (Fig. 2.) Older wanderers, ripe for a new stage of development as fixed cells, have abundance

That which is real and permanent in the individual, is thus to be conceived of as an integral portion of that divine Self Who subsists at once both as an infinite whole, and in infinite sub-division.

9. It is hardly necessary to elaborate on this point or to provide more expert opinions. It is enough to say that this internal method of interpreting sacred writings was, and still is, the method used by all who possess the <term>Gnosis</term> <note>From the Greek word for "knowledge"; specifically refers to a direct, mystical understanding of spiritual truths rather than mere belief.</note>, or secret knowledge of the mysteries. They leave the literal meaning to the uneducated and to the "critics," seeing it only as the husk or shell. This outer layer serves only to hide, protect, and preserve the life-giving seed—the priceless pearl of the true "Word" of God.

10. Both the story of the Fall and all related myths or parables are much older and more universal than the average reader of the Bible realizes. The Bible itself, in its Hebrew form, is a relatively recent collection and adaptation of ancient mysteries. The central scenes of these mysteries were carved on temple walls and written or painted on papyrus scrolls long before the time of Moses. Furthermore, history informs us that the Book of Genesis as it exists today is not even the work of Moses. Instead, it is the work of Ezra (also called Esdras), who lived during the Captivity <note>The Babylonian Captivity (approx. 597–538 BCE), during which the Jewish people were exiled to Babylon; Ezra is traditionally credited with reconstituting the Jewish law and scriptures afterward.</note>—between five and six hundred years before our era. He is said to have recovered these and other writings through the process previously described as <term>Intuitional Memory</term> <note>The concept that an individual can "remember" spiritual or historical truths from a past existence or from a collective divine source through deep meditation.</note>. "My heart," he says, "overflowed with understanding, and wisdom grew in my breast; for *my spirit strengthened my memory*." <note>A reference to the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras 14:40.</note> If he used such means to recover what Moses had previously given to Israel by word of mouth, it is obvious that Esdras must have been initiated into that ancient tradition in a previous lifetime. No amount of *memory* could have allowed him to recover something he had never known—knowledge which, when the Divine command to rewrite it was given to him, was so completely lost that "no man knew any..."

# THE FALL.

This heavenly Fire <note>In this context, "Fire" refers to the divine spark or the vital life-force of the spirit.</note> is in the spiritual part of man. But Prometheus <note>A figure from Greek mythology who stole fire from the gods; here, he represents "pseudo-thought" or the intellect when it is disconnected from spiritual truth.</note> or pseudo-thought—the spurious thought as opposed to the true <term>Hermetic reason</term> <note>The "Hermetic reason" refers to a higher, spiritual intellect named after Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of ancient wisdom traditions.</note>—steals or "draws down" this Fire from its original place and transfers it to the outer man or body. Thenceforward, the consciousness of man ceases to reside in the soul, and takes up its abode in the body. That is to say, that man in his "fallen" condition is conscious only of the selfhood of the body, and until regenerate <note>Spiritually reborn or restored.</note>, or redeemed from the "Fall," he does not again become conscious and vitalised in the soul. To find the Soul is the first step towards finding Christ; that is, as the Catholic Church puts it, "*Mary brings us to Jesus.*" <note>An allegorical interpretation where Mary represents the Soul that gives birth to the Divine Spirit (Jesus) within the individual.</note> 

The materialistic unregenerate man is totally unconscious of his soul. He is aware only of the body, and his percipience of life is limited to the bodily sense. This act is the <term>Promethean Theft</term> <note>The misuse of divine creative energy for purely physical or selfish purposes.</note>, punished so terribly by the "Father" at the hand of Hermes, the true Thought, or <term>Angel of Understanding</term>. ### PART IV.

31. We now reach the last and innermost interpretation of our fourfold hieroglyph <note>A "hieroglyph" here refers to a sacred symbol or myth that contains multiple layers of meaning.</note>, the spiritual and creative secret embodied in the Edenic allegory. This secret is sometimes more obscurely alluded to as the Lapse of heavenly beings from their first happy estate into sub-celestial spheres, and their final redemption by means of penance done through incarnation in the flesh. It need scarcely be said that this imagined Lapse is also a parable designed to veil and preserve a truth. ### PART I.

1. OUR subject is again the cataclysmal event mystically called the <term>Fall of Man<gloss>In this context, the "Fall" is not a historical event involving a literal fruit, but a spiritual decline where the human soul becomes preoccupied with the material world rather than the divine.</gloss></term>. Before entering upon it, we will recapitulate briefly what has been said respecting the nature of man. As already explained, this is fourfold <note>The authors follow a mystical tradition that views the human being as a "tetrad," or a four-part system, mirroring the structure of the universe.</note>. This fourfold nature is itself included in a dual personality. Consisting of male and female, <term>Reason<gloss>The masculine, analytical aspect of the mind.</gloss></term> and <term>Intuition<gloss>The feminine, direct perception of spiritual truth.</gloss></term>, Man is, in this sense, a twofold being. But the masculine <term>moiety<gloss>one of two parts or halves</gloss></term> comprises the dualism of Sense and Intellect; and the feminine moiety, the dualism of Soul and Conscience.

2. Owing to this duality of his constitution, every doctrine relating to Man has, primarily, a dual significance and application. And owing to his fourfoldness, it has also, secondarily, a fourfold significance and application. The interpretation, therefore, of any doctrine must, to be complete, be at the least twofold. And since there is between the inner and outer spheres of man’s being an exact <term>correspondence<gloss>A central Hermetic principle: "As above, so below." The belief that patterns in the physical world reflect patterns in the spiritual world.</gloss></term>, by virtue of which, whatever subsists or occurs in the one sphere has its counterpart in the other, the terms which describe the one apply also to the other; and no interpretation or application is complete which does not include both spheres.

<summary>This page defines the "fourfold nature" of humanity—consisting of Reason, Intuition, Sense, and Soul—as the foundation for understanding the Fall. It argues that because humans are dual-natured, all spiritual doctrines must be interpreted through both an internal (spiritual) and external (physical) lens.</summary>

3. Thus it comes,—to quote a fragment of <term>Hermetic derivation<gloss>Teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure representing ancient Egyptian and Greek mystical wisdom.</gloss></term>,—that:—

> *All Scriptures which are the true Word of God, have a dual interpretation, the Intellectual and the Intuitional, the Apparent and the Hidden.*
>
> *For nothing can come forth from God save that which is fruitful.*
>
> *As is the nature of God, so is the Word of God's Mouth.*
>
> *The Letter alone is barren; the Spirit and the Letter give Life.*
>
> *But that Scripture is the more excellent which is exceeding fruitful; and brings forth abundant signification.*
>
> *For God is able to say many things in one; as the perfect Ovary contains many seeds in its Chalice.* <note>The author uses botanical metaphors—the ovary and chalice—to describe how a single divine word can hold the "seeds" of many different meanings.</note>
>
> *Therefore there are in the Scriptures of God's Word, certain Writings which, as richly yielding Trees, bear more abundantly than others in the self-same holy Garden.*
>
> *And one of the most excellent is the Parable of the Fall, which, as a stream parted into four branches, has a fourfold head, and is a word exceeding rich.* <note>The "four branches" likely refer to the four rivers flowing out of Eden (Pishon, Gihon, Tigris, and Euphrates), which the authors interpret as symbols of the fourfold nature of man: physical, emotional, intellectual, and spiritual.</note>

For a parable it is, and not a history, as ordinarily understood; but having a hidden, that is, a mystic meaning;—a parable, moreover, which, while founded indeed upon a particular fact, is true for all time, in that it is perpetually being enacted. Being thus, the Parable of the Fall constitutes an **Eternal Verity**. <note>original: "Aeterna Veritas." A truth that is not just true in the past, but is a fundamental law of human existence in every moment.</note>

4. The opening chapters of the sacred books exhibit, then, not merely events occurring in, and having relation to, a particular place or time, but the meaning and object of religion at large, the creation of man, the nature of sin, and the method of salvation; and all these as perpetually subsisting. These chapters constitute thus a kind of...

5. For, in the <term>Divine Mind<gloss>The universal consciousness or intelligence of God.</gloss></term>, there is no past; in the Divine economy, no future. God is *I AM*, and always *IS*. <note>This refers to the name of God revealed to Moses in Exodus 3:14, "Ehyeh asher Ehyeh," signifying eternal existence.</note> For this reason, the Hebrew, or sacred language, is all in one tense; <note>The authors are referring to a mystical view of the Hebrew language where the "perfect" and "imperfect" tenses are seen as describing completed or ongoing actions in a way that transcends linear time.</note> and the Scriptures are a perpetual record of that which is always taking place. Thus, the Spirit of God, which is original Life, is always moving upon the face of the waters, or heavenly deep, which is original Substance. And the One, which consists of those two, is always putting forth alike the <term>Macrocosm<gloss>The "Great World"—the entire universe or cosmos.</gloss></term> of the universe and the <term>Microcosm<gloss>The "Little World"—the individual human being, viewed as a reflection of the universe.</gloss></term> of the individual, and is always making man in the image of God, and placing him in a garden of innocence and perfection, the garden of his own unsophisticated nature. And man is always falling away from that image and quitting that garden for the wilderness of sin, being tempted by the serpent of sense, his own lower element. And from this condition and its consequences he is always being redeemed by the blood of the sacrifice always being made for him by the Christ Jesus, who is Son at once of God and of man, and is always being born of a pure virgin;—dying, rising, and ascending into heaven.

6. For these are, one and all, mystic terms denoting facts of perpetual recurrence in the history of the Soul, and necessary to salvation. It depends, however, upon the sense in which they are understood, whether they minister to salvation or to condemnation. The letter, it is declared, killeth; <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6: "the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life."</note> the letter and the spirit together have and confer life. For, while interpreted in one sense,—the sense of the spirit,—they are divine truths; interpreted in another sense,—the sense of the letter,—they are idolatrous falsehoods.

And inasmuch as <term>idolatry<gloss>The error of mistaking a physical symbol for the spiritual truth it represents.</gloss></term> consists in the <term>materialisation<gloss>The process of turning abstract or spiritual concepts into concrete, physical objects.</gloss></term> of <term>spiritual mysteries<gloss>Sacred truths that are hidden from the ordinary senses and understood only through the soul.</gloss></term>, and the substitution for the true things signified, of their material symbols; those interpretations are idolatrous which give to <term>mystical doctrines<gloss>Teachings concerning the direct, internal experience of the divine.</gloss></term> physical applications. Now, all <term>Scripture<gloss>Sacred writings, specifically the Bible.</gloss></term> given by <term>inspiration<gloss>Literally "divine breath"; the belief that human writers were guided by a divine influence.</gloss></term> of God is mystical; and, in its <term>esoteric sense<gloss>The inner or hidden meaning intended only for those with specialized knowledge.</gloss></term>, deals not with material things, but with <term>spiritual realities</term>, the mystic intention of the things named being alone implied, and by no means the things themselves. And this rule holds good alike of those two divisions of Scripture which are called respectively the <term>Old and the New Testament</term>.

7. In accordance, then, with the fourfold constitution of existence, the <term>Parable of the Fall<gloss>The story of Adam and Eve’s exile from Eden, interpreted here as a symbolic journey of the soul rather than a historical event.</gloss></term> has a <term>fourfold signification<gloss>A meaning that exists on four distinct levels: spiritual, moral, intellectual, and physical.</gloss></term>. But, inasmuch as that which is true of the race is true also of the individual, and that which is true of the individual is true also of the race, each portion of the fourfold signification has a twofold application, namely, to the race and to the individual. For each alike it is true on the <term>planes spiritual, moral, intellectual, and physical<gloss>The different layers of reality, ranging from the highest divine essence to the densest material form.</gloss></term>. And it is constructed in terms derived from this last, because only thus it can find on any plane universal recognition;—since the physical is the universal mirror of the <term>unmanifest<gloss>The divine source or reality that exists before or beyond physical form.</gloss></term>, and is the only medium capable of reflecting at once all the three planes above itself. Thus represented in terms derived from the physical, it possesses a meaning for all, if only as an <term>allegory of the Seasons<gloss>A symbolic story where the changes in nature represent deeper spiritual or psychological cycles.</gloss></term>, for---having an <term>astronomical basis<gloss>Founded on the movements of stars and planets, which the authors believe mirror spiritual laws.</gloss></term>---such it also is.

8. So far, however, from being intended to represent the actual natural history, either of the planet or of man, or to be what now-a-days it is the fashion to call scientific, it is so contrived as to make that history appear to be the reverse of what it really is. For, read by the superficial <note>The text ends here mid-sentence, suggesting that the "superficial reader" is the one who mistakes these allegories for literal, scientific history.</note>

...because to the soul, Matter is a forbidden thing. <note>In this philosophical system, "Matter" refers to the lowest, most dense state of existence, which is the opposite of the soul's divine, spiritual nature.</note> So that the act constitutes a disobedience. The prohibition, however, is not an arbitrary one, but is founded in the soul's own nature, as also is the penalty attached to her transgression. Only by remaining spiritual substance can soul subsist as soul, having all the potentialities of soul. By quitting her own proper condition and descending into Matter, she takes upon herself the limitations of Matter. As between <term>Spirit and Matter<gloss>The two poles of existence: Spirit is the infinite, creative essence, while Matter is the finite, created form.</gloss></term> there is no boundary line, it is only by the maintenance of a will set exclusively spirit-wards, that a soul can be held from subsiding into the lower condition of Matter, finally to disintegrate and perish.

17. That only which perishes is the *individuality* constituted of these. And it perishes through its own persistent refusal of that "**Gift of God**" which is **Eternal Life**, the gift, namely, of a portion of God's Self or Spirit. Refusing this, man refuses life, as he is free to do. God rejects and annihilates no one. Man, by his rejection of God, annihilates his own individuality. And God cannot make man on any other terms. And this, for the reason that God is omnipotent. <note>The author argues that if a person could remain a separate, immortal individual while being in opposition to God, they would be a second God, which would negate God's all-encompassing power.</note> God would not be omnipotent were the individual indestructible. For then there would be something not God, possessing all the power of God. So far from this doctrine being an impugnment of the Divine love and goodness, it is essential to these qualities. God, we have said, rejects and destroys nothing. But there is in things evil an element of self-destruction, in the operation of which lies the safety of the universe. ### PART II.

<margin>*</margin> 19. The full significance of the <note>Referring to the story of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden.</note> Parable under consideration, and the unity of the <term>mystic Scriptures<gloss>Sacred texts when read for their inner, symbolic, and spiritual meanings rather than their literal historical claims.</gloss></term>, become conspicuously apparent when we collate their various corresponding utterances, as by taking into account those also of the Book of Revelation. For **Mysticism**, on the contrary, existence,—or, more properly, <term>Being</term>,—and consciousness are terms synonymous and interchangeable; and all **Substance**, under whatever mode manifested, continues still to be, in some mode, consciousness. And the Church—which is the collective soul of Humanity—fell in the same way an individual soul does: by looking less and less upward toward God and more and more downward toward Matter. However catastrophic the result may seem when we look at the total effect from a distance of time, the **decline** <note>original: "declension"</note> was actually very gradual and took place over many generations. It can be compared to a decrease in a farm's harvest, like what happens when the soil is slowly exhausted. The spiritual potential of the human race had, in a sense, spent itself. Or, it can be compared to the receding of the tides or the changing of the seasons. For until a person is finally joined to God through what is mystically called the **Divine Marriage** <gloss>The ultimate state of spiritual union where the individual soul is perfectly aligned with the Divine Will.</gloss>, humanity is subject to many shifts and fluctuations in its spiritual condition. # LECTURE THE EIGHTH.

## *THE REDEMPTION.*

### PART I.

1. **THAT**, then, which, mystically, is called the **Fall of Man** <note>In this mystical context, the "Fall" is not a historical event involving a literal Adam and Eve, but a psychological shift where the human spirit loses its mastery over the physical senses.</note>, does not mean, as commonly supposed, the lapse, through a specific act, of particular individuals from a state of original perfection; nor, as sometimes supposed, a change from a fluidic <note>Referring to an ethereal or purely energy-based state of existence.</note> to a material condition. It means such an inversion of the due relations between the soul and the body of a personality already both spiritual and material, as involves a transference of the central will of the system concerned, from the soul—which is its proper seat—to the body, and the consequent subjection of the soul to the body, and liability of the individual to sin, disease, and all other evils which result from the limitations of **Matter** <term>Matter: here understood as the most dense and limited state of existence, which traps the spirit when the will is focused solely on the physical.</term>.

2. That, therefore, which, mystically, is called the **Redemption** <note>The process of "buying back" or reclaiming the soul's rightful authority over the physical body.</note>, and which is the converse of the Fall, does not mean, as commonly supposed, the remission <note>remission: the formal cancellation of a debt, penalty, or punishment.</note>, or transference from the guilty to the innocent, of the penalties incurred through the Fall. No penalty incurred by man ever is or can be remitted by God, since the Divine Justice is *just*. Nor, for the same reason, can it be borne by another, since a substitution of the innocent for the guilty would in itself be a violation of justice. Wherefore the doctrine of

**Vicarious Redemption** <note>The traditional church doctrine that Jesus Christ died as a substitute for sinners, satisfying God's justice by taking their punishment upon himself.</note>, as ordinarily accepted, represents a total misconception of the truth, and one derogatory to the **Divine Character**. The **Redemption** means such removal of the will of the individual system concerned, from the body, and reinstatement of it in the soul, as thenceforth to secure to the soul full control over the body, and to exempt the individual from further liability to transgression. He who is redeemed cannot sin, that is, mortally <note>In this context, "mortally" refers to sins that lead to the death or extinction of the soul's progress.</note>.

3. It is according to the **Divine order of Nature** that the soul should control the body. For, as a manifested entity, man is a **dual being**, consisting of soul and body; and of these, in point both of duration and function, and therefore in all respects of value, the precedence belongs to the soul. For the soul is the real, permanent **Individual**, the **Self**, the everlasting, substantial **Idea**, of which the body is but the temporary residence and **phenomenal expression** <term>phenomenal expression: a temporary appearance in the physical world of senses, as opposed to an eternal, spiritual reality.</term>. The soul, nevertheless, has, properly speaking, no will of her own, since she is feminine and negative <note>The author uses "feminine" in the Hermetic or mystical sense, meaning the soul is a vessel or "receptive" principle that must be directed by a "positive" or masculine will—either the Spirit or the Flesh.</note>. And she is therefore, by her nature, bound to obey the will of some other than herself. This other can be only the **Spirit** or the **Body**;—the **Within and the Above**, which is Divine, and is **God**; or the **Without and the Below**, which, taken by itself and reduced to its last expression, is the "**devil**" <note>This defines the "devil" not as a personified being, but as the lowest state of matter and external focus, separated from spiritual influence.</note>. It is, therefore, to the Spirit and soul as one, that obedience is due. Hence, in making the body the seat of the will, the man revolts, not merely against the soul, but against God; and the soul, by participation, does the same. Of such revolt the consequence is disease and misery of both soul and body, with the liability, ultimately, to extinction of the soul as well as of the body. The doctrine which regards the universe as the **Thought of God**, is a true doctrine. But the universe is not therefore unsubstantial. **God** is real **Being**, and that which **God** thinks is also **God**. Wherefore in consisting of the thought of the **Divine Mind**, the **Universe** consists of the **Substance** of that **Mind**, the **Substance**, that is, of **God**.

Put forth by, and, in a sense divided from, **God**, in order to accomplish **God’s** purposes, these become *messengers* of **God**, that is, **Angels**. ### PART III.

24. In assigning to the Gospels their proper meaning, it is necessary to remember that, as mystical <term>Scriptures</term> <note>Derived from the Latin *scriptura*, meaning "writings," used here to denote texts with a hidden, spiritual depth.</note>, they deal, primarily, not with material things or persons, but with spiritual significations. Like the “books of Moses,” therefore, and others which, in being mystical, are, in the strictest sense, prophetical, the Gospels are addressed, not to the outer sense and reason, but to the soul. And, being thus, their object is, not to give an historical account of the physical life of any man whatever, but to exhibit the spiritual possibilities of humanity at large, as illustrated in a particular and typical example. The design is, thus, that which is dictated by the nature itself of Religion. For Religion is not in its nature historical and dependent upon actual, sensible events, but consists in processes, such as <term>Faith</term> <note>Understood here as an internal spiritual perception rather than a mere intellectual belief in facts.</note> and <term>Redemption</term> <note>The process of being liberated from the lower, material self and restored to a spiritual state.</note>, which, being interior to all men, subsist irrespectively of what any particular man has at any time suffered or done. That alone which is of importance, is what God has revealed. And therefore it is that the narratives concerning Jesus are rather parables founded on a collection of histories, than any one actual history, and have a spiritual import capable of universal application.

30. There is, moreover, a yet further explanation of the indifference to identity of detail by which everywhere this narrative is characterized. Being four in number, and arranged in an order corresponding to that of the four divisions of man's nature, the **Gospels** have for their standpoint, and bear relation to, different regions of existence. 

Thus, the **Gospel of Matthew**, which represents the lower and physical plane, appeals more particularly on behalf of the character ascribed to **Jesus of Nazareth** as fulfilling the promises of the <term>Messiah</term> <note>The "Anointed One" prophesied in Hebrew scripture; here interpreted as a state of spiritual attainment.</note> of the Old Testament, and is pervaded by one principle: the fulfilment in him at once of the Law and of the prophecies.

The **Gospel of Luke** represents the further ascent to the plane of the **soul** and the **intuition**. Hence it occupies itself chiefly with accounts of the spiritual parentage of the <term>Man Regenerate</term> <note>A person who has fully integrated their physical, intellectual, and spiritual selves into a perfected state.</note>—setting forth under a <term>parabolic narrative</term> <note>A story intended to illustrate a spiritual or moral lesson rather than record literal history.</note> his genesis from the operation of God in a pure soul. To the same end, this Gospel gives prominence to the familiar conversations, rather than to the formal teaching of its Subject, since it is in these that the affectional nature of a man is best manifested.

### PART IV.

31. In every part of the world of antiquity exist memorials of the Sacred Mysteries <note>Secret religious rites of the ancient world where initiates were taught spiritual truths through symbolic dramas and rituals.</note> and tokens of the ceremonials which accompanied initiation into them. The scene of these ceremonials was generally a subterranean labyrinth, natural or artificial, the object being to symbolise the several acts in the Drama of Regeneration <note>The process of spiritual rebirth or transformation, where a person moves from a purely physical existence to a higher spiritual state.</note> as occurring in the interior and secret recesses of man’s being. The Catacombs of Rome, used for similar purposes by the early Christians, were suggestive of the same idea, though this was not the immediate motive for the selection of such a retreat to be the home of the infant Church. And explorers of the passages under the Great Temple of Edfou <note>A significant Egyptian temple dedicated to the god Horus, known for its extensive inscriptions and underground chambers.</note> relate how, after traversing with extreme difficulty a tunnel thirty inches high and forty-two inches wide, they emerge into a large hall adorned with a profusion of sacred paintings and hieroglyphs. Similar excavations have been found at Hermione in Greece, Nauplia, Gadara, Ptelion, Phyle, and other places. And all accounts agree in stating that the Mysteries were variously celebrated in pyramids, pagodas, and labyrinths which were furnished with vaulted rooms, extensive wings, open and spacious galleries, and numerous secret caverns, passages, and vistas, terminating in mysterious *<term>adyta</term>* <note>original Latin/Greek: "adyta," meaning the innermost, most sacred sanctuaries of a temple, which were closed to the public.</note>. And in describing a catacomb in Upper Egypt, called *<term>Biban el Moluk</term>* <note>original Arabic: "Bībān al-Mulūk," meaning the "Gates of the Kings," now commonly known as the Valley of the Kings.</note>, Belzoni <note>Giovanni Battista Belzoni (1778–1823), a pioneering Italian explorer and archaeologist of Egyptian antiquities.</note> mentions an alabaster chest deposited therein, which, though surmised by him to have been intended as a sarcophagus <note>A stone coffin, typically adorned with sculpture or inscriptions.</note>, resembled rather the coffers used in the religious celebrations for which such labyrinths were designed. 42. IT was no part of the design of the Gospels to represent either the course of a man perfect from the first, or the whole course from the first of the man made perfect. # LECTURE THE NINTH.

## *GOD AS THE LORD; OR, THE DIVINE IMAGE.*

### PART I.

1. **ALL** sacred books, of whatever people, concur in adopting in respect of the <term>Deity<gloss>The essential nature of God or a supreme being.</gloss></term> two apparently opposite and antagonistic modes of expression. According to one of these modes, the <term>Divine Being<gloss>The ultimate reality or Godhead.</gloss></term> is external, universal, diffused, unformulated, indefinable, and altogether inaccessible and beyond perception. <note>This refers to the "transcendence" of God—the idea that God is completely outside and beyond the physical universe.</note> According to the other, the Divine Being is near, particular, definite, formulated, personified, discernible, and readily accessible. <note>This refers to "immanence"—the idea of God dwelling within the world and the human soul.</note> Thus, on the one hand it is said that God is the high and holy One that inhabiteth eternity, and is past finding out; that no man hath seen God at any time, neither heard God’s voice, or can see God and live. <note>These phrases reference several biblical passages, including Isaiah 57:15, Job 11:7, and John 1:18.</note> And, on the other hand, it is declared that God has been heard and beheld face to face, and is nigh to all who call upon God, being within their hearts; and that the knowledge of God is not only the one knowledge worth having, but that it is open to all who seek for it; and the pure in heart are promised, as their supreme reward, that they shall “see God.” <note>A reference to the Beatitudes in the Gospel of Matthew 5:8.</note>

2. Numerous instances, moreover, are recorded of the actual <term>sensible vision<gloss>A vision that can be perceived by the senses, whether physical or spiritual, appearing as a concrete form rather than just an abstract feeling.</gloss></term> of God. Of the Hebrew prophets, Isaiah says that he saw the Lord “high and lifted up”; <note>Isaiah 6:1.</note> Ezekiel, that he beheld the “glory of the God of Israel” as a figure of fire; <note>Ezekiel 1:26-28.</note> Daniel, that he beheld God as a human form, <note>Daniel 7:9-13, describing the "Ancient of Days."</note>

6. This utterance contains both a statement and a mis-statement of the doctrine with which we are now concerned. An analysis of it will therefore minister to the desired elucidation. The truth in it is, that “the Lord is God manifested as a man;” for in “the Lord,” the Formless assumes a Form, the Nameless a Name, the Infinite the Definite, and these human. Before specifying the error, it may be remarked that, admirable seer as was Swedenborg, he was, nevertheless, too much under the influence of prevailing habits of life and thought, to be an infallible interpreter. Having neither physically nor mentally undergone the purification indispensable to the production of a perfect instrument, his mind was no <note>original: "tabula rasa"</note> blank slate <gloss>A mind in its primary state, free from preconceived ideas or impressions.</gloss> to the impact of the celestial. Hence, great as was the advance he made on all previous attempts at interpretation, the improvement was in respect of method far more than of results. And not

## PART II.

11. It is necessary to devote a brief space to an exposition of the ancient and true doctrine in respect of the place and value of the Understanding in things religious. For so we shall both further minister to the rehabilitation of this supreme faculty, and exhibit the extent to which <term>sacerdotalism<gloss>A system where the priesthood acts as a necessary intermediary between God and humanity, often emphasizing ritual over personal understanding.</gloss></term> has departed from the right course. Mention has already been made of Hermes as the “*trainer of the Christs*.” <note>original: "paedagogus Christorum"</note> The phrase is identical with those more familiar phrases which describe Christ as the “*Son of David*” and as the “*Seed of the Woman*”; and, in short, with all statements respecting the genealogy of the Christ, including the declaration that the Rock on which the Church of Christ is built is the Understanding. For of all such statements the meaning is, that the doctrine represented by the term Christ,—so far from being a Mystery, in the sacerdotal sense,—is a truth necessary and self-evident, and requiring for its discernment as such, only the full and free exercise of *Thought*. Now, this term *Thought* is no other than the name of the Egyptian equivalent of Hermes, the God *Thaut*, frequently written *Thoth*; these being for the Greeks and Egyptians respectively the personification of the Divine Intelligence. It has already been stated that in the Celestial all properties and qualities are Persons, the fact being that it is always in the guise of a person that the Divine Spirit of a man holds intercourse with him, the mode adopted on the occasion corresponding to the function to be exercised. Thoth and Hermes are, then, names expressive of the personality assumed by the supreme <term>Nous<gloss>Greek for "Mind" or "Intellect"; in this context, the highest faculty of spiritual perception.</gloss></term> of the <term>Microcosm<gloss>Meaning "the little world"; the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</gloss></term> when operating especially as the Intelligence or Understanding.
